content: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a prevalent developmental disorder that typically begins in childhood and can persist into adulthood. It is characterized by a combination of hyperactive and poorly regulated behaviors, along with significant inattention. Over time, ADHD can negatively impact academic performance, career achievements, and social-emotional development. Meditation has been increasingly utilized as a therapeutic approach for various psychological conditions. It is hypothesized that meditation could serve as a tool for improving attentional control in individuals with ADHD. To evaluate the effectiveness of meditation therapies for ADHD, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, ERIC, PsycINFO, and others, covering literature from their inception up to January 2010. The search also included grey literature and trial registries. The review focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that assessed the efficacy of meditation therapies in children or adults diagnosed with ADHD. Data extraction was performed independently by two authors using a standardized form. Additional information was sought from study authors when necessary. The treatment effects were analyzed using mean difference (MD) as the statistical measure, and the findings were presented in tables, figures, and narrative descriptions. The review included four studies with a total of 83 participants. Two studies employed mantra meditation, while the other two utilized yoga. These interventions were compared against drug therapy, relaxation training, non-specific exercises, and standard treatment controls. However, the studies exhibited significant design limitations, leading to a high risk of bias. Only one of the four studies provided data suitable for statistical analysis. In this study, no statistically significant differences were observed between the meditation therapy group and the drug therapy group on the teacher-rated ADHD scale (MD -2.72, 95% CI -8.49 to 3.05, 15 participants). Similarly, no significant differences were found between the meditation therapy group and the standard therapy group on the teacher-rated ADHD scale (MD -0.52, 95% CI -5.88 to 4.84, 17 participants). Additionally, there was no statistically significant difference between the meditation therapy group and the standard therapy group in a distraction test (MD -8.34, 95% CI -107.05 to 90.37, 17 participants). Due to the limited number of studies, small sample sizes, and high risk of bias, no definitive conclusions can be drawn regarding the effectiveness of meditation therapies for ADHD. Furthermore, no adverse effects of meditation were reported in the included studies. Additional, well-designed trials are necessary to provide more robust evidence on this topic.
